headline: 5G network, blind spots covered: Delhi government nod to 5 call-blocking towers at prisons
content: An inmate attempting to make a call from an illegally-held mobile phone from inside the jail may receive a signal on his device but the call does not go through. Instead, the system alerts telecom service providers with the IMEI number of the mobile phone, helping prison authorities identify and recover the device. This is how the Towers of the Harmonious Call Blocking System (T-HCBS) works. The system is designed to block unauthorised mobile communication across 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G networks without disrupting mobile connectivity in areas surrounding the prison complex. At present, among the city’s three prison complexes, Tihar, which has nine jails, has two such towers on its premises. While Mandoli has one, Rohini does not have any. Now, for the first time, the system will cover entire prison premises and will be equipped to block the 5G network, according to sources. The Delhi government has approved Rs 6.12 crore for installing five additional advanced call-blocking towers across the three prison complexes — one at Tihar, two at Mandoli and two at Rohini. Decreases dependence on unreliable jammers According to officers, the primary function of these towers is to prevent inmates from using unauthorised mobile phones while enabling authorities to identify the devices being used inside prison premises. “The pseudo-technology creates the illusion of a mobile network on an inmate's handset. When the inmate attempts to make a call, it does not connect to the intended recipient. Instead, it helps the telecom service provider identify the mobile phone being used inside the jail complex. The service provider then shares the phone’s IMEI details with the jail administration, helping officials recover the illegal device,” an officer said. Until now, prison authorities have largely depended on mobile jammers, an outdated technology that blocks mobile signals indiscriminately, affecting connectivity in areas surrounding the prison complexes as well, officers said. “These towers will also have a white-listing facility, under which telecom service providers can be informed about specific mobile numbers that should not be blocked. These will include numbers used by prison staff and people living in areas surrounding the prison complexes,” a source said. Gaps addressed An officer said the HCBS was first tested at Mandoli Jail in January 2020 using a temporary mobile tower. Subsequently, two such towers were installed in Tihar and one in Mandoli. However, officers added that the existing system has not been fully effective because the towers do not cover the entire prison premises, leaving a few blind spots and also limited to 4G networks. Some mobile phones had been recovered from both prison complexes using the system. The installation of additional towers is expected to improve coverage across the Tihar and Mandoli complexes, officers said. Sources said the approval was granted by the Home (General) department following a proposal submitted recently by the Prison department. Each tower is estimated to cost around Rs 1.22 crore, taking the total tentative expenditure to Rs 6.12 crore. The Prison Department will separately bear the electricity costs required to operate the system. Further checks According to an official source, the move is part of the government's efforts to prevent inmates from using mobile phones to carry out illegal activities from inside prisons. The technology upgrade will be accompanied by stricter monitoring of prison staff and inmates to prevent security lapses. “Technology alone is not enough, so we are strengthening human vigilance as well. Home Minister Ashish Sood has instructed prison officials to conduct regular surprise checks, rotate staff duties and enforce strict preventive measures,” a source said. The department has also been directed to strengthen ground-level surveillance through regular inspections and measures to prevent mobile phones from being smuggled into prison premises, the source added. An officer said the proposed installation builds on efforts that began in 2019, when a specialised committee was constituted to develop an alternative to conventional mobile jammers. Since traditional jammers can interfere with mobile networks outside prison premises, authorities had been exploring a system that can restrict unauthorised communication within jail boundaries without affecting surrounding areas. Sood has directed the Prison department to follow the General Financial Rules, 2017, Government e Marketplace (GeM) procurement guidelines and vigilance norms while executing the project. It has also emphasised transparency and compliance with prescribed financial procedures, officers said.

headline: CISCE Holds First National Student Mental Health Conclave, 90 Delegates From 18 Regions Participate
content: The Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations (CISCE) has organised its first National Student Mental Health and Well-Being Conclave 2026, bringing together 72 student delegates and 18 teacher delegates from 18 regions to discuss adolescent mental health and ways to make schools more supportive and emotionally safe. The three-day conclave was held from November 20 to 22 at the CISCE Centre of Excellence in Hyderabad. According to CISCE, the event aimed to put students at the centre of discussions on mental health by giving them an opportunity to share their experiences, identify emerging concerns and contribute to recommendations for schools. The national-level event was the culmination of a three-tier initiative involving school-level discussions, virtual regional conclaves across 18 regions and national deliberations. The wider initiative was designed to engage nearly 16 lakh students from Classes 6 to 12, more than 32,000 teachers and over 3,300 affiliated schools. The discussions focused on four areas: student stress and academic pressure; emotional well-being, digital life and positive relationships; drug and substance abuse and healthy choices; and building resilience and encouraging help-seeking behaviour. The programme included thematic discussions, expert-led sessions, collaborative workshops and a panel discussion. Experts from academia, industry and professional practice facilitated the sessions. CISCE said the deliberations would contribute to four national-level outcomes: a Student Mental Health Charter, a Student Well-being Index, a Repository of Best Practices and a White Paper on Emerging Mental Health Concerns among Adolescents. CISCE Chief Executive and Secretary Dr Joseph Emmanuel said a student-centred education system must begin by listening to learners and translating their concerns into institutional commitments and responsive school practices. The council said student delegates would return to their respective schools and regions as ambassadors of mental health and well-being, sharing the insights and recommendations from the conclave. Aradhna Chand, school counsellor and psychology educator at St Thomas School, Jagadhri, Haryana, highlighted the importance of creating a sense of connection, safety and belonging for children’s emotional, academic and digital well-being. Student delegates also shared their experiences of participating in the conclave. Yashraaj Saha of Holy Cross School, Agartala, said the event made him feel that his voice mattered, while Aradhya Singh of Lucknow Public College said she returned with greater self-awareness, friendships and new perspectives on emotional well-being. CISCE said the conclave marked a shift from discussions about student well-being to actively involving students in shaping school-level approaches to mental health.

headline: NGT directs Sangrur DC to act on poor waste management
content: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has directed the Sangrur Deputy Commissioner (DC) to take immediate remedial measures to address the city’s deteriorating municipal waste management system and submit an action taken report within four weeks.The NGT's Principal Bench in New Delhi expressed serious concerns over the situation and directed the DC to personally oversee the processing of legacy waste and the implementation of proper solid waste management measures.The directions were issued on November 18 during the hearing of Original Application Number 613/2025 (Kamal Anand vs State of Punjab and others). The Bench was headed by NGT Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and Expert Member Dr Afroz Ahmad.The tribunal also took note of administrative instability in the Municipal Council, Sangrur. During the proceedings, the Additional Deputy Commissioner, who appeared virtually, informed the Bench that former Executive Officer Ashwini Kumar had left the job and a new incumbent was expected to join.Despite the change in leadership, the NGT stressed that accountability could not be compromised. The administration assured the tribunal that the DC would directly supervise waste management operations.One-month deadlineThe administration informed the tribunal that notices had been issued to bulk waste generators defaulting on waste management norms within the municipal limits. As the notice period had expired, the civic authorities were directed to initiate penal action against the non-compliant entities within one month.Recover penaltiesThe tribunal also expressed concern over the recovery of environmental compensation imposed on the Municipal Council, Sangrur.The environmental compensation (EC) imposed on the civic body stands at Rs 92 lakh, of which only Rs 18 lakh has been deposited.Similarly, against environmental damage compensation (EDC) of Rs 84 lakh, only Rs 18 lakh has been recovered.The NGT directed the DC to ensure recovery of the outstanding amounts within four weeks and submit a comprehensive action taken report.The matter will next be taken up by the tribunal in February 2027.

headline: After Class 10 Textbook Complaint, NCERT Issues Strict Advisory To Printers
content: A day after assuring strict action over complaints of blurred and tiny text in a Class 10 textbook, the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has issued a formal advisory to all its empanelled printing presses, directing them to strictly follow prescribed quality standards and technical specifications. In an advisory issued by its Publication Division on Monday, NCERT said it had taken serious note of concerns regarding compromised printing quality and substandard textbooks. The council has directed all empanelled printing presses to maintain the required standards and ensure proper inspection and quality control at every stage of printing and production. The advisory emphasises strict compliance with NCERT’s prescribed technical specifications, quality standards and production guidelines. It also calls for maintaining quality in printing, colour reproduction, registration, finishing, binding and overall workmanship. NCERT has warned that any deviation from the prescribed specifications, negligence in maintaining quality standards or supply of substandard books will be viewed seriously. The advisory lists possible action against printing agencies found violating the prescribed standards. These include penalties, rejection of supplies, cancellation of allotted work, termination of contracts, revocation of empanelment and debarment or blacklisting, wherever applicable under the relevant tender conditions and contractual provisions. In a post on X, NCERT said it had issued the strict advisory following concerns over compromised printing quality and substandard textbooks. The council reiterated that quality was non-negotiable when it came to educational resources. Ensuring Quality in Every Book! Taking serious note of concerns regarding compromised printing quality and substandard NCERT textbooks, the NCERT Publication Division has issued a strict advisory to all empanelled printing presses. The advisory emphasises strict adherence to prescribed quality standards, technical specifications, proper inspection and quality control at every stage of printing and production. Quality is non-negotiable when it comes to educational resources. Read the Advisory: https://t.co/VvDertJrrM #NCERT #NCERTTextbooks #QualityEducation #PublicationDivision #Education — NCERT (@ncert) November 23, 2026 The latest advisory follows a complaint about the readability of a Class 10 NCERT History textbook, in which the text was allegedly blurred and too small to read comfortably. Advocate Vineet Jindal had flagged the issue in a post on X, and raised concerns that prolonged reading of textbooks with such printing defects could lead to eye strain, headaches and other health-related problems among schoolchildren.

headline: Waqf Board opposes plan to remove Krishi Bhawan mosque for Central Vista project
content: The Delhi Waqf Board (DWB), asserting its claim related to the Krishi Bhawan mosque which is planned for removal owing to the Central Vista Redevelopment project, has told the Delhi High Court that any action by the Centre against the mosque without considering the Board’s statutory role “would be premature and legally unsustainable”. The DWB’s stance comes after a petition was filed by a worshipper last week accusing the Board of not abiding by its statutory duties to protect the mosque. Another petition was filed by the Krishi Bhawan mosque’s managing committee Qadeemi Masjid before the Delhi HC in September, apprehending demolition of the mosque. The apprehension arose after a tender was floated by the Central Public Works Department (CPWD), under the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), on January 19 for the construction of Common Central Secretariat (CCS) buildings 4 and 5, at the site of Krishi Bhavan and Shastri Bhawan. The Centre had earlier told the court that the Waqf-notified mosque, which occupies about 111 square yards within the precincts of Krishi Bhawan, will be removed and is “impermissible and incompatible with the secular character of Government property”. The DWB has, however, contested the Centre’s stance. In a reply dated November 14, it denied that reserving space for the mosque is inconsistent with the Master Plan or the secular character of the property. Joining the managing committee as well as a worshipper, who are seeking protection of the mosque and that due process be followed for any action against the mosque, the DWB has urged the court to restrain the Centre “from taking any coercive steps for demolition, removal, dispossession, sealing, or permanent discontinuance of religious activities at Masjid Krishi Bhawan, except in accordance with law”. While asserting that “no decision concerning demolition, removal, relocation or permanent discontinuance of religious activities should be taken” without “consideration of the Board’s objections and compliance with the procedure prescribed by law”, the Waqf Board has also emphasised that public interest does not override statutory status. “.proposed redevelopment of the Central Secretariat complex, including the construction of Common Central Secretariat Buildings 4 and 5, cannot, by itself, be treated as sufficient justification for disregarding the notified status and religious character of Masjid Krishi Bhawan..public interest and infrastructure development, though legitimate governmental objectives, must be pursued in accordance with law. Such objectives cannot automatically override the statutory status of a notified Waqf property or the applicable constitutional protections,” it said. Meanwhile, on Monday, Justice Anish Dayal while hearing the pleas, urged the Centre to consider an amicable solution while citing examples of airports and cantonments which have multifaith prayer facilities. Justice Dayal, addressing ASG Chetan Sharma, representing the Centre, remarked, “See if it can be considered, only for the purposes of employees (of Krishi Bhawan). These are your employees, they are government employees.we are a country of many faiths.” While ASG Sharma responded that the government may look at “a situation where government employees who wish to pray can be accommodated”, he made it clear that “it cannot be open for public”. ASG Sharma further proposed, “We have to apply our mind in this. It could be that this petition (by Qadeemi Masjid) as well as the other one (by worshipper) can be taken as representation through the Delhi Waqf Board.” Notably, the worshipper had made representation to the DWB on November 15 and to the Land and Development Office (L&DO) of Centre on November 16. Justice Dayal directed the DWB as well as the L&DO to “give a response in writing within 6 weeks” to the representations. The court further clarified that the responses are being elicited for the purpose of assisting the court with the adjudication of the matter. The court will hear the matter next on January 14.

headline: ‘Can’t leave to doctors’: Calls for support system for children with Type 1 diabetes
content: From spotting early signs to access to Insulin and awareness in schools — experts called for a wider societal support system for children with Type 1 diabetes on Monday as HRIDAY, a civil society organisation, organised an event titled ‘Beyond Diagnosis: Living Well with Type 1 Diabetes at Home, in Schools and Communities’ at All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Delhi. The event brought together endocrinologists, government representatives, people suffering from the condition, caregivers, teachers and civil society groups. Sam Gulati, who has Type 1 diabetes, was a teenager when he was diagnosed with the condition. An Executive Director at Tata Technologies, he is now 36, married, and has a daughter. “It was a shock to my parents and me when I was diagnosed in 2006, and the initial years were tough and lonely,” he said. He takes four doses of Insulin a day. “Glucose monitoring was hard. My Insulin use was irregular,” he recalled. What made it easier was support from other people. “I would come to AIIMS and talk to patients to understand the disease better. My parents did the same in the OPD, talking to other parents, long conversations about this condition. Gradually, I was introduced to a community through the Yogdhyan Foundation, and I got holistic support,” he recollected. The cost of the treatment was another challenge. “But we somehow sailed through the initial years.” The awareness sessions, he added, made the difference. “They helped my parents and me understand the condition and manage its impact.” His was one of the many heartening accounts of struggles shared at the event. Four Ts that can save a child Experts pointed out that the recently revised Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) 2.0 Operational Guidelines, 2026 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) bring symptom-based screening for Type 1 diabetes in children up to 18 years in focus. Known as the ‘4Ts’, four warning signs — ‘Toilet, Thirsty, Tired and Thinner’ — were flagged. These refer to passing urine more often, constant feeling thirsty, unusual tiredness and unexplained weight loss. Under the guidelines, suspected cases get a random blood glucose test and a referral to the non-communicable disease clinic at the district hospital. The guidelines also provide for risk-based screening for Type 2 diabetes among adolescents. Stressing on early diagnosis and recognition, Dr Nikhil Tandon, Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism at AIIMS, said, “Early diagnosis and recognition matters because Type 1 diabetes can turn life-threatening if missed. It is an autoimmune disease, simply, the body makes little or no Insulin. Unlike Type 2, it is not mainly tied to lifestyle. He further added, “The approach has to be different from Type 2. Type 1 diabetes happens in children. It can be managed with proper treatment, and that treatment is Insulin. And the condition needs testing and constant monitoring.” He urged civil society to help build awareness among parents, teachers and schools. “As a society, there needs to be greater awareness and understanding of Type 1 diabetes. Teachers and parents need to spot the warning signs and know what to do, because children spend most of their day away from hospitals. “ “It cannot be left to doctors and healthcare professionals alone,” he said. He also stressed the need for policy action at national and international levels, and for better implementation of national guidelines. RBSK 2.0, he said, is a chance to improve early identification and referral. The disease goes to school along with the child For a child with Type 1 diabetes, treatment is not limited to hospitals. Insulin management , glucose level monitoring , proper and timely meals and an active lifestyle. “Insulin management, regular blood glucose monitoring, healthy nutrition and physical activity are essential components of everyday care,” Tandon said. That means families who know how to help. It means schools where a child can check glucose, or simply keep Insulin in the school fridge, take Insulin, and join class and sport without stigma. Prof. Monika Arora, Executive Director, HRIDAY, said, "Children need an enabling environment in which healthy routines and diabetes care become part of everyday life. Schools, families, health systems and communities all have a role in building awareness and reducing stigma.” The event also showcased 'The Grassroots to Global India Initiative', led by HRIDAY with partner organisations, which works to raise awareness, connect people to care and build community support. Its first phase reached more than 1.4 million people, said the organisers. The second phase has reached around two lakh so far.

headline: Uttar Pradesh State Bio-Energy Policy, 2022: Incentives, eligibility and implementation
content: POLICY AT A GLANCEItemPositionOfficial titleUttar Pradesh State Bio-Energy Policy, 2022Cabinet approvalSeptember 27, 2022Government orderOctober 3, 2022Policy validityFive years from notificationAdministrative departmentDepartment of Additional Sources of Energy, Uttar PradeshNodal agencyUttar Pradesh New and Renewable Energy Development Agency (UPNEDA)Main eligible projectsCompressed biogas, bio-coal, biodiesel and specified bio-energy projects; UPNEDA portal also covers second-generation bioethanolCBG subsidyRs 75 lakh per tonne of production capacity, capped at Rs 20 croreBio-coal subsidyRs 75,000 per tonne of production capacity, capped at Rs 20 croreBiodiesel subsidyRs 3 lakh per kilolitre of production capacity, capped at Rs 20 croreBiomass-collection equipment30 per cent state subsidy, capped at Rs 20 lakh, in addition to eligible Union government supportStamp duty100 per cent exemption on qualifying land transactionsElectricity duty100 per cent exemption for ten yearsDevelopment charges100 per cent exemptionGovernment landMay be leased at Re 1 per acre per year for eligible projects and feedstock storageImplementation statusState reported 53 projects approved and 24 established by 2025The policy promotes conversion of agricultural residue, livestock waste, municipal waste and other biomass into commercial energy products. It replaced the State Bio-Energy Policy, 2014 and the State Bio-Energy Enterprise Promotion Programme, 2018. What is the Uttar Pradesh State Bio-Energy Policy?The policy is a five-year framework for attracting private investment into waste- and biomass-based energy projects.Its principal focus is on:Compressed biogas (CBG);Bio-coal;Biodiesel;Other approved waste-based bio-energy technologies.UPNEDA's current project-registration portal additionally lists second-generation bioethanol among the types of bio-energy projects it processes.The policy is intended to address two linked problems. Uttar Pradesh produces large quantities of agricultural residue, livestock waste, municipal solid waste and by-products from sugar mills. Much of this material can create environmental problems if burnt, dumped or otherwise poorly managed. At the same time, it can serve as feedstock for fuels and energy products.The policy therefore seeks to create a commercial market for waste while providing farmers and rural enterprises with an additional source of income. Why was the policy introduced?The earlier State Bio-Energy Enterprise Promotion Programme, 2018 offered capital subsidy, State Goods and Services Tax reimbursement and stamp-duty relief. According to the 2022 policy, 14 projects had received sanction letters under that programme.The state nevertheless concluded that a revised policy was needed because of:Burning of agricultural residue in fields;Loss of soil fertility associated with residue burning;Availability of livestock waste;Municipal solid waste requiring productive utilisation;Agricultural-market waste;Waste generated by sugar mills;Demand for cleaner substitutes for fossil fuels;Potential additional income for farmers;Rural employment opportunities.The 2022 framework therefore shifted emphasis towards commercially scalable production of CBG, bio-coal and other biofuels.Its five-year validity applies from notification. Units registered and commissioned under the policy remain entitled to approved benefits for the period prescribed for their projects even where those benefits extend beyond the policy's five-year registration window. Which projects can qualify?The policy applies to eligible new bio-energy plants and also allows benefits where new plant and machinery are installed in an already registered unit, subject to the applicable conditions.The main project categories are:Compressed biogasCBG is produced by processing organic material such as cattle dung, agricultural residue, press mud, municipal organic waste and similar biodegradable feedstock. The resulting biogas is purified and compressed to a quality suitable for fuel applications.The policy supports projects linked with Union government initiatives such as the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation programme, or SATAT. Holders of Letters of Intent under relevant central programmes may participate in the state framework after completing the prescribed state registration and project documentation.Bio-coalBio-coal is a solid fuel manufactured from biomass residues and can substitute partly for fossil coal in suitable industrial and power-generation applications.The policy encourages private bio-coal projects, including projects linked with thermal-power facilities where suitable land and commercial arrangements are available.BiodieselThe policy supports biodiesel production and envisages use of non-edible oilseed crops where appropriate.It specifically refers to plants such as karanj, neem, castor and jatropha, particularly on barren or infertile land, as possible supplementary feedstock sources.BioethanolThe current UPNEDA registration portal includes second-generation bioethanol as a bio-energy project category. However, the headline production-linked state subsidy specified in the 2022 policy provides explicit rates for CBG, bio-coal and biodiesel, not a comparable per-unit rate for bioethanol. A bioethanol developer should therefore verify the specific scheme or sanction applicable to its project rather than applying the biodiesel rate by analogy.What subsidy is available for compressed biogas?A qualifying CBG project may receive state assistance calculated at Rs 75 lakh per tonne of production capacity, subject to a maximum of Rs 20 crore per unit.This is a production-capacity-linked capital subsidy rather than a payment of Rs 75 lakh for every tonne actually sold each year.For example, the headline calculation for a plant with sufficient eligible capacity could theoretically exceed Rs 20 crore, but the policy ceiling restricts the state subsidy to Rs 20 crore.The subsidy may be used towards approved expenditure on:Plant and machinery;Infrastructure;Construction;Power-supply infrastructure;Transmission-related works.The cost of the administrative building and land is specifically excluded from the subsidy calculation.What subsidy is available for bio-coal?Eligible bio-coal plants may receive Rs 75,000 per tonne of production capacity, capped at Rs 20 crore per unit.As with CBG, this is not a subsidy paid continuously for every tonne sold. The approved plant capacity forms the basis for determining the eligible amount.A bio-coal project must also demonstrate reliable biomass availability. Agricultural residue used for briquettes, pellets or similar fuels has competing uses, including animal fodder, domestic fuel and soil management. Feedstock planning is therefore part of project viability.What subsidy is available for biodiesel?The policy provides assistance of Rs 3 lakh per kilolitre of eligible biodiesel production capacity, subject to the same overall ceiling of Rs 20 crore per unit.Biodiesel developers must separately comply with applicable Union government fuel-quality, blending, sale and environmental requirements.The state subsidy is stated to be additional to benefits available under relevant Government of India schemes, subject to the rules against duplicate reimbursement of the same expenditure.When is the capital subsidy released?The policy requires the detailed project proposal to be examined by subject experts before the government's subsidy liability is determined.The capital subsidy is released into the unit's bank loan account after commencement of commercial production, subject to the approved terms and verification.This distinction is important for investors. The policy does not provide the Rs 20 crore maximum as an upfront amount for constructing a plant.A developer must arrange:Promoter equity;Bank or institutional finance;Land;Construction expenditure;Machinery;Working capital;Statutory approvals;before relying on the state subsidy.What support is available for collecting agricultural residue?A bio-energy plant can operate only if sufficient biomass reaches it at commercially viable cost. Collection, baling and transport of crop residue are therefore important elements of the policy.For eligible biomass-collection equipment such as balers, rakers and trolleys, the state provides a subsidy of 30 per cent, capped at Rs 20 lakh.The state assistance is in addition to the subsidy available under the Government of India's agricultural mechanisation programme, under which the policy refers to support of up to 50 per cent for qualifying machinery.The arrangement is intended particularly to facilitate aggregators and organisations involved in biomass collection, including eligible farmer producer organisations and cooperatives.The state subsidy should not be interpreted as a guarantee that 80 per cent of every equipment purchase will be reimbursed. Eligibility under the central and state components must be assessed separately.How does the policy address feedstock availability?Feedstock risk is one of the biggest commercial challenges for a bio-energy project.The policy provides for assessment of available waste and biomass before registering plant capacity. It seeks to avoid allowing projects to consume all locally available residue because biomass is also required for other uses.The framework therefore restricts registration of waste-based bio-energy capacity in a tehsil with reference to the estimated local feedstock and energy-generation potential.The policy also envisages supplementary energy crops on barren and infertile land, including:Karanj;Neem;Castor;Jatropha;Sweet sorghum;Energy grasses.Farmer producer companies and rural entrepreneurs can participate in developing these feedstock value chains.A plant developer should nevertheless undertake an independent feedstock study covering seasonal availability, procurement radius, competing uses, moisture content, storage and transport costs.Is government land available?Yes. The policy permits eligible government land to be made available for bio-energy plants and feedstock collection or storage at a token lease rent of Re 1 per acre per year, subject to availability and government approval.The policy framework provides for leases of up to 30 years under the applicable land-allotment process.This is not an automatic right to any government parcel chosen by an investor. The land must:Be available with the competent department;Be suitable for the project;Be formally allotted;Be used for the approved purpose;Meet environmental and development conditions.The state also issued subsequent revenue-department orders to facilitate implementation of the land provisions. UPNEDA's government-order repository continues to list these implementation measures.What stamp-duty benefit is available?Eligible bio-energy enterprises receive 100 per cent stamp-duty exemption on qualifying land acquired through purchase or lease from private landholders for:Establishing the bio-energy plant; orFeedstock collection and storage.The Stamp and Registration Department formally notified the exemption on April 12, 2023.It covers the eligible conveyance or lease instrument under the conditions prescribed in the notification.Applicants should complete the prescribed certification before registration rather than assuming that stamp duty paid without following the notified process will automatically be refunded later.What electricity-duty and development-charge benefits are available?Eligible bio-energy enterprises receive 100 per cent exemption from electricity duty for ten years from commencement of commercial production.This does not mean electricity itself is free. The plant remains liable for energy charges, demand charges and other non-exempt components of its electricity bill.The policy also provides 100 per cent exemption from development charges levied by state development authorities.Separate government orders were subsequently issued to operationalise this exemption.Is infrastructure support available?For a qualifying bio-energy investment of at least Rs 50 crore, the policy provides for assistance with construction of an approach road connecting the project to the main road, for a distance of up to 5 km, subject to the applicable Public Works Department provisions.Invest UP's policy page lists a separate government order implementing the Public Works Department component of the policy.This should not be treated as a Rs 50 crore road subsidy. Rs 50 crore is the qualifying project-investment threshold; the actual infrastructure work depends on the approved road requirement and departmental process.What land-use facilitation is provided?The policy provides regulatory facilitation for conversion and use of land needed for qualifying projects.Invest UP summarises the framework as providing deemed permission under relevant change-in-land-use and land-ceiling provisions, subject to the implementation orders issued by the Revenue Department.This does not waive environmental, building, fire or pollution-control approvals.A CBG or biodiesel facility may still require approvals relating to:Pollution control;Fire safety;Factory operation;Storage of fuels or gases;Electrical systems;Pressure equipment;Water use;Waste handling;Local development requirements.How can an investor apply?UPNEDA operates a dedicated Bio Energy Portal for registration of projects. Applicants can register a proposed plant, submit the request to UPNEDA, track its status, respond to queries and lodge grievances through the portal.The broad process is:Select the bio-energy technology and proposed capacity.Identify a reliable feedstock source.Prepare a detailed project report.Arrange land or seek eligible government land.Register the project on the UPNEDA Bio Energy Portal.Submit feedstock, technology, financing and land documents.Obtain the required Letter of Interest or project registration.Secure statutory permissions and bank finance.Construct and commission the project.Begin commercial production.Submit verified capital-expenditure and capacity documentation.Claim the applicable state subsidy and exemptions.UPNEDA also publishes implementation guidelines and subsequent government orders on its portal.Implementation and progress so farThe policy remains actively listed on Invest UP, Nivesh Mitra and the UPNEDA Bio Energy Portal in 2026.Official Uttar Pradesh government material published in 2025 reported that 53 projects involving compressed biogas, bio-coal, biodiesel or bioethanol had been approved, of which 24 projects had been established.These figures are more meaningful than investment proposals alone because the government explicitly distinguishes approved projects from those established. However, "established" should still not automatically be interpreted as full rated production unless project-specific commissioning and output data are available.The official sources reviewed did not provide a consolidated current dashboard showing:Production capacity of all 24 established projects;Actual CBG, bio-coal or biodiesel output;Capital subsidy sanctioned and disbursed by project;Feedstock collected annually;Farmer payments generated;Electricity-duty and stamp-duty benefits utilised;Employment created specifically under the policy.Accordingly, approved projects, established plants and actual commercial output should continue to be reported separately.Key challenges and practical considerationsFeedstock security: Plants need reliable year-round biomass or waste supplies.Seasonality: Agricultural residue availability can vary sharply through the year.Transport cost: Low-density biomass can become expensive to move over long distances.Competing uses: Crop residue may already be used for fodder, fuel or other industries.Offtake risk: CBG, bio-coal and biodiesel projects need dependable commercial buyers.Working capital: Feedstock often has to be purchased and stored before fuel is sold.Environmental compliance: Waste-based projects still require rigorous pollution and safety management.Post-production subsidy: Investors must finance project development before state capital assistance is released.FAQsWhat is the maximum subsidy for a CBG plant?Rs 75 lakh per tonne of eligible production capacity, capped at Rs 20 crore per unit.What does a bio-coal plant receive?Rs 75,000 per tonne of eligible production capacity, subject to the Rs 20 crore ceiling.What is the biodiesel incentive?Rs 3 lakh per kilolitre of eligible production capacity, capped at Rs 20 crore.Is agricultural-residue collection equipment subsidised?Yes. The state provides 30 per cent assistance up to Rs 20 lakh on specified machinery, in addition to eligible Union government support.Is government land available?Eligible government land may be leased at Re 1 per acre per year, subject to availability and approval.Is stamp duty exempt?Yes. Qualifying purchase and lease transactions receive 100 per cent stamp-duty exemption.Which agency implements the policy?UPNEDA, under the Department of Additional Sources of Energy. ConclusionThe Uttar Pradesh State Bio-Energy Policy, 2022 combines production-capacity-linked subsidy with land, tax and infrastructure support to turn agricultural and other organic waste into commercial energy.Its headline incentive reaches Rs 20 crore per project for eligible CBG, bio-coal and biodiesel units. The policy also provides ten-year electricity-duty relief, full stamp-duty and development-charge exemptions, low-cost government land and assistance with biomass-collection machinery.Official data showing 53 approved projects and 24 established projects indicate measurable implementation. The next test is whether those plants operate sustainably, secure reliable feedstock, generate fuel at commercial scale and provide additional income to farmers. Policy performance should therefore be judged by actual production and subsidy disbursement rather than project approvals alone. SourcesUttar Pradesh State Bio-Energy Policy, 2022, Department of Additional Sources of Energy, Government of Uttar Pradesh.Bio-Energy Enterprises Promotion Programme, 2022, Invest UP, Government of Uttar Pradesh.Bio Energy Portal, Uttar Pradesh New and Renewable Energy Development Agency.Bio-Energy Policy Government Orders and Implementation Guidelines, UPNEDA.Stamp-duty notification under the Uttar Pradesh State Bio-Energy Policy, 2022, Government of Uttar Pradesh; April 12, 2023.Policies and Government Orders, Invest UP, Government of Uttar Pradesh.

headline: Parties step up campaign for civic body repoll
content: Campaigning for the Municipal Corporation, Patiala, re-polls has gathered momentum, with leaders of the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), the Opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) and the Congress holding nukkad sabhas and leading door-to-door campaigns in the 30 poll-bound wards.As many as 165 candidates — 30 each from the AAP, the BJP, the SAD and the Congress, besides 45 Independents — are in the fray for the 30 wards, which will go to the polls on November 28, two years after the general municipal elections.The BJP and other opposition parties had alleged electoral malpractices, rigging, booth capturing and widespread violence during the previous general elections. They subsequently approached the Supreme Court, which, on October 7, ordered fresh elections in 30 wards.While the ruling AAP is reaching out to voters with a list of the Punjab Government's achievements in sanitation, public health and civic infrastructure, the opposition parties have centred their campaigns on allegations of corruption, the drug menace and poor civic amenities. Garbage management and the inadequate maintenance of natural drains in the city have also emerged as key campaign issues.Addressing party workers and booth managers campaigning for AAP candidate Rupali Arora in Ward No. 57, Patiala Mayor Kundan Gogia urged them to ensure maximum voter turnout and motivate residents to cast their votes before lunchtime on polling day.He also addressed a nukkad sabha in support of party candidate Jyoti in Ward No. 45 on Monday.Gogia described the re-polls asan opportunity for party workers to prepare for the 2027 Assembly elections. "We must repeat the success of the 2022 Assembly elections.The municipal elections will help us strengthen our organisational base and test our preparations," he said. A senior BJP leader and party's women's wing president Jai Inder Kaur has been actively campaigning for party candidates, with the BJP eyeing a larger share in the 60-member House. The party currently claims the support of five councillors.

headline: Patiala: Young voters urged to exercise their franchise
content: Divisional Commissioner-cum-Roll Observer Vinay Bublani today held a meeting with the Patiala MP, MLAs from all Assembly constituencies, representatives of political parties and all Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to review the ongoing Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls with January 1, 2027, as the qualifying date.Deputy Commissioner-cum-District Election Officer Himanshu Jain and ADC Anuprita Johal were also present.Appealing to all political parties to actively cooperate in the revision process, Bublani said that every eligible voter, particularly young voters, should come forward to vote.Sharing the SSR schedule as per Election Commission of India guidelines, he said that the draft electoral rolls were published on November 12, while claims and objections can be submitted till December 11. Special camps will be organised on November 22 and December 6, and claims and objections will be disposed of by December 28.The final electoral rolls will be published on January 4, 2027, followed by a meeting with political parties. As per the draft electoral rolls published on November 12, Patiala district has 14,34,888 voters, including 7,34,438 males, 7,00,404 females and 46 third-gender voters.Following rationalisation, the number of polling stations has increased from 1,861 to 1,864. Between September 13 and November 23, the district received 30,337 applications under Form 6, 120 under Form 6A, 8,408 under Form 7 and 16,485 under Form 8.Issuing directions to EROs, Bublani stressed proper training of BLOs and supervisory officers, preference for appointing local BLOs and adequate availability of Forms 6, 6A, 7 and 8.He directed officials to organise SVEEP activities, special registration camps in educational institutions for young voters. He ordered timely disposal of all applications and re-verification of the 20 polling stations with the highest number of additions and the 20. He appealed to political parties to facilitate the registration of all eligible citizens who fulfil the January 1, 2027 qualifying criteria. Form 6 is meant for new voter registration, Form 6A for overseas Indian voters, Form 7 for deletion of names and Form 8 for corrections and shifting of residence.

headline: National Health Mission staff protest hits OPD, lab services in Bathinda
content: The protest by employees of the National Health Mission (NHM) outside the Civil Surgeon’s office in Bathinda entered its 14th day on Monday, with workers continuing their agitation over long-pending demands.The employees staged a district-level demonstration against the state government and submitted a memorandum to the Civil Surgeon, requesting that it be forwarded to the government through the proper channel.The NHM Employees’ Union, Punjab, is demanding the regularisation of contractual employees and implementation of the principle of equal pay for equal work.Union leaders said NHM employees had been serving in the Health Department for several years, but the government had failed to take a concrete decision on their demands, forcing them to launch the protest.The ongoing strike has affected OPD-related work, laboratory services, and both online and offline operations at government health institutions across the district.The employees’ union leaders warned that the agitation would be intensified if their demands were not accepted. They said employees could resort to a hunger strike and, if necessary, even a fast unto death to press for the fulfilment of their demands.

headline: Patiala: College holds seminar on Parkash Purb of Guru Nanak Dev
content: Khalsa College, Patiala, organised a series of programmes, including an academic seminar and a humanitarian service initiative, to commemorate the sacred Parkash Purb of Guru Nanak Dev.The programmes were organised by the Department of Religious Studies, the Kirat Club and the Department of English and Foreign Languages to spread awareness about the teachings of Guru Nanak Dev and promote the values of compassion, selfless service and helping the underprivileged.During the seminar, Maninder Singh presented a research paper highlighting the life and teachings of Guru Nanak Dev, while Balraj Singh shared his insights on the topic, "A Philosophical Study of Sidh Gosht".

headline: As Punjab farmer unions open doors, Opposition steps up to woo them for polls
content: With the Punjab Assembly elections barely three months away, two leading state farm unions have decided to extend their support to the Sukhbir Singh Badal-led Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) in the polls, marking a shift from the farmer bodies' traditional stance of keeping a distance from political parties. On November 2, the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Kadian), a Doaba-based farm union, decided to back the SAD, with its president Harmeet Singh Kadian making the announcement at a joint press conference with Badal in Chandigarh. After a fortnight, on November 18, the BKU (Lakhowal), a Malwa-based farm outfit, also declared its backing to the Akali Dal after Badal visited the residence of its president Ajmer Singh Lakhowal in Ludhiana. Farm politics These developments have not only boosted the SAD's moves to strengthen its connect with the farm community in the run-up to the 2027 elections, but have also brought the political equations concerning the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM) into focus again. Formed in 2020, the SKM is an umbrella organisation of a slew of Punjab farmer unions, which had spearheaded the farm agitation during 2020-21 on Delhi's borders against the now-repealed three central agricultural laws. Partap Singh Kadian, father of Harmeet Singh Kadian, had been elected as an SAD MLA in 1968. Also, BKU (Mann) leader Bhupinder Singh Mann had been a Rajya Sabha member from 1990 to 1996, nominated as an MP by the President in recognition of his work in the farm movement. Mann has maintained that he was a nominated member without any affiliation to any party. Mann's outfit had, however, extended its support to the Congress in the 2002, 2012 and 2017 Assembly elections besides the 2019 Lok Sabha polls. "Farmer unions have by and large tried to remain apolitical, but at times a few unions have openly supported political parties," said Jagmohan Singh Patiala, an SKM leader. Patiala also said, “It was in 1989 that the BKU started facing splits. Once Bhupinder Singh Mann went to the Rajya Sabha, the split happened quickly. Earlier, all farmer leaders were under one platform. Later, several farm unions were formed, including BKU (Lakhowal), BKU (Dakaunda), BKU (Ugrahan), etc," he said. Oppn outreach The moves by the two SKM constituents, BKU (Kadian) and BKU (Lakhowal), to back the Akali Dal have triggered speculation about some other farm unions looking to align with various Opposition parties for the 2027 elections, even as the Congress is also set to reach out to them. "If a number of farm unions are extending support to the SAD, what happens if the party enters into an alliance with the BJP? Will these unions then indirectly support the BJP as well, a party because of which many farmers died on the Delhi borders while protesting against the central farm laws?" asked Narian Dutt of the Inqlaabi Manch, a social organisation. BKU (Lakhowal) general secretary Harinder Lakhowal said,"If BJP agrees to our demands, what is the harm. People have formed the government of the Congress thrice as well after the 1984 Operation Blue Star and Sikh massacre. And, in the 2022 elections, farmers voted overwhelmingly for the AAP." For Ajmer Lakhowal, extending support to the SAD has not marked a new political association. He had been the Punjab Mandi Board chairman from 2007 to 2017, when the SAD-BJP coalition was ruling the state. Reacting to Lakhowal's decision to join hands with the SAD, the ruling AAP's general secretary Baltej Pannu said, "Lakhowal had served as the Mandi Board chairman, but did not raise any issues concerning farmers during his tenure. When the farmers' agitation began in 2020, Lakhowal pushed his son Harinder Lakhowal to the forefront of the movement. Now that Lakhowal is extending support to the SAD, he should explain what he had done for the welfare of farmers earlier, and what good he proposes to do for them now.” The AAP has been at the receiving end of farm unions' protests over the last few years on various issues, with the unions accusing the Bhagwant Mann-led party government of failing to fulfil its various promises for their welfare and empowerment. “Direct support to the AAP is unlikely, at least for now. There is no doubt that farmer unions are being increasingly approached by the Opposition parties. It remains to be seen whether the Congress is able to garner farm unions' support for the 2027 polls, depending on its vision for safeguarding farmers' interests,” a union leader told The Indian Express. The BJP, too, is intensifying its outreach to farmers, with Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan making repeated visits to Punjab to connect with farmers and others associated with the agricultural sector. Farm unions' play Ahead of the 2022 Assembly elections, the SKM had expelled about 22 farmer unions after they decided to form the Sanyukt Samaj Morcha (SSM) to contest the elections. The SSM's emergence also led to the formation of the SKM (non-political) organisation to oppose the farm unions' foray into politics. The SSM, however, failed to win any of the state's 117 seats, following which it became politically inactive. The SKM (non-political)'s convener Jagjit Singh Dallewal said: "We formed our organisation because our ideology doesn't match with supporting political parties or contesting polls. Now that two unions have supported the SAD, it is their individual decision, but what happens if the SAD ties up with the BJP?" Asked how farm unions could extend support to a party while being part of the SKM, Harmeet Kadian and Harinder Lakhowal claimed that the SKM has amended its rules to allow its constituents to make independent electoral choices. "After the 2022 polls, most SSM unions rejoined the SKM. Now we have amended the rules to allow a farm union to extend support to any political party. We are not contesting the polls. But we, too, are voters and have the right to decide our choices," they said. Kadian said that if an individual member of a union contests an election, the member would not be allowed to participate in the SKM meetings, while other members of that union could continue to attend them. Accusing the AAP and the Congress of not addressing their concerns, Kadian added: "Considering all this, we feel that a regional party like the SAD, which upholds Sri Akal Takht Sahib, can alone safeguard the interests of Punjab farmers”.

headline: Patiala: Punjabi University scholar wins BRICS award
content: Punjabi University research scholar Dr Akashpreet Kaur has brought laurels to the institution by winning the prestigious 9th BRICS Young Innovator Prize 2026 for her research on a self-powered cardiac pacemaker.A post-doctoral fellow in the Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering at Punjabi University, Dr Akashpreet is working under the supervision of Prof. Sonia Goyal. The award was presented during the BRICS Young Scientist Forum and Young Innovator Prize held at the National Institute of Advanced Studies (NIAS), Bengaluru, last week.The event witnessed participation from young researchers and innovators from India, Russia, Brazil, China, the UAE and Iran. Each participating country was allowed to nominate a maximum of three candidates, while the entries were evaluated by an international jury comprising one expert from each of the six participating nations.Dr Akashpreet was among only two candidates selected to represent India at the event. She presented her research on a self-powered cardiac pacemaker that harnesses energy generated by the natural movement of the heart to operate implantable cardiac devices.Congratulating the research scholar and her supervisor, the Vice-Chancellor Dr Jagdeep Singh said the achievement reflected the university’s strong research environment and academic excellence. Prof. Sonia Goyal said the award-winning work had its origins in Dr Akashpreet’s PhD research at Panjab University, Chandigarh. The research was conducted under the guidance of Dr Gaurav Sapra, Associate Professor, Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, UIET, and Dr Ankur Gupta, Cardiologist at PGIMER, Chandigarh.

headline: Ashok Gehlot interview: ‘Bhajan Lal Sharma suits us. Let him remain CM’
content: The Congress swept the Rajasthan rural elections on November 20, dealing a blow to the ruling BJP. Former CM and one of the Opposition party’s senior-most leaders, Ashok Gehlot speaks to The Indian Express about its performance, why he thinks there will be no more infighting, why he does not want CM Bhajan Lal Sharma replaced, and backlash over Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s comments abroad, among other issues. Excerpts: * What is your takeaway from the rural election results? There is some impact of what is happening around the country on the results. A large number of people from Rajasthan attended the (INDIA bloc) rally against “vote chori” in Delhi. So, the mood was against the BJP in the state. People have realised that democracy in the country is in danger. Also, there is the proposed delimitation, which is as dangerous as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). As they did in Assam, they played the same game in the Rajasthan local body polls. They clubbed the four-five wards in which we are strong as boards are formed on the basis of the number of wards you win. Then there are local factors at play. * What kind of local factors are you referring to? Within six to eight months after the BJP government was formed, people realised that it cannot deliver good governance and that it is not serious. People across the state are complaining that their work is not being done, while pointing out that corruption is on the rise. Even BJP supporters are saying this. If a pradhan or an MLA from the BJP is saying this, where will people go? Hence, there was anger against the government. To top this, the government published advertisements comparing its performance to the previous (Congress) government. First, it was one year versus five years, then two years versus five years and now, it is three years versus five years. However, there was nothing concrete done on the ground. All these factors – the national mood and anger at the local level – worked in our favour. People have taught them a lesson. It was their third anniversary gift to the government. * Do you think the CM’s position is vulnerable after the BJP's rout? The situation in Rajasthan is such that the rural and local body polls were held after the judiciary was forced to step in. The government was not keen on holding elections as it is scared. When the Nagar Nigam polls took place, the BJP was ahead by 0.9 percentage points, that too after large-scale irregularities, including the misuse of bureaucracy and a flawed delimitation. BJP supporters said (Chief Minister) Bhajan Lal Sharma was good. Now, the same people will say he is baggage. What can we say? ‘Hume toh yahi suit karte hai. Rahe, wahi rahe (He suits us. Let him stay)’. * How is the contest for the coming elections shaping up, in your view? Based on the reports coming in, even from Uttar Pradesh, people are against the government. In Punjab, some people say the Congress can even win, while the situation is good in Uttarakhand. Unemployment and price rise are big issues; so is the government’s attempt to carry out delimitation. The same issues are being raised by Gandhi and (Congress president) Mallikarjun Kharge both in and outside Parliament. People are seeing this. I can say with confidence that change will begin from Rajasthan. In 2028, we will win the state convincingly. It will be a one-sided election which will herald a change at the national level. * In the past, the Congress has been accused of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Kharge too once said the Congress needs to translate favourable public mood into electoral victories … A few days ago, all top leaders attended a meeting at the state Congress office. (State Congress chief) Govind Singh Dotasra, (state LoP) Tika Ram Jully, and (AICC general secretary) Sachin Pilot were present. I had said then that we are united. People always say there is infighting in the Congress. You will not be able to say that again. There will be no more infighting in the Congress. We approached the local body polls with a united mindset. We will move forward unitedly, as this is no longer ‘about the party’. It is ‘about the country’. I say we must remain united in national interest. If the BJP wins in 2029 (Lok Sabha elections), you never know if there will be elections after that. India could have elections like Russia or China. If the Opposition weakens further, it will not bode well for democracy. Moreover, the bitterness between the government and the Opposition is unprecedented. The Centre introduced the Delimitation Bill (package) without involving or consulting the Opposition. It also did not convene an all-party meeting on the issue. * Rahul Gandhi has been called an anti-national over remarks he made abroad… All this will not work now. Everybody knows that family. No member of that family has held any position of Prime Minister, Chief Minister or minister in the last three and a half decades. Despite the people of the country believing in the family, the BJP talks about dynasty. We will continue to follow the Congress’s principles and policies despite what the BJP says.

headline: Government allots Lutyens’ Delhi bungalow to the Dalai Lama
content: The Union government has provided a Lutyens’ Delhi bungalow, barely three kilometres away from its seat of power, to the Dalai Lama, The Indian Express has learnt. The bungalow, on 20, Pandit Ravi Shankar Shukla Lane, has been renovated over the past few months. When The Indian Express visited the area on Monday, the nameplate of “Gaden Phodrang” was visible at the entrance of the bungalow, while construction debris could be seen outside. Gaden Phodrang is the office of the Dalai Lama that was registered as a trust when the Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leader decided to relinquish political authority in 2011. The Dalai Lama is the chairman of the trust. “Following His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s voluntary devolution of political authority to a democratically elected Tibetan leadership in 2011, the Gaden Phodrang — the Office of His Holiness the Dalai Lama — was registered as a private trust under the Indian Registration Act of 1908. This registration was carried out with the Sub-Registrar in Dharamsala to formally establish it as a legal entity in India. The trust is dedicated to preserving and upholding the institution of the Dalai Lama and his spiritual work, while advancing his humanitarian vision,” the Dalai Lama’s official website says. According to sources, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has provided the bungalow for the Dalai Lama. Last year, the MEA had written to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) seeking a bungalow, though it was not mentioned who it would be allotted to. The MoHUA had transferred the Type 7 bungalow to the MEA in October 2025 for “operational” purpose. The MEA spokesperson did not respond to an email sent by The Indian Express on Monday in this regard. In July this year, the Central Public Works Department, which maintains the bungalow, had floated a tender of Rs 34.94 lakh for the installation of security features, including “provision of porta cabin, strengthening of peripheral boundary wall, concertina coil fencing…strengthening of gates etc.” According to the Dalai Lama’s website, he had “reaffirmed” on May 21, 2025 that the institution of the Dalai Lama would continue and the Gaden Phodrang Trust would be primarily responsible for recognising the 15th Dalai Lama, his successor. “The Trust will be responsible for overseeing the identification, education, and well-being of future Dalai Lamas in accordance with Tibetan Buddhist traditions. Beyond its spiritual responsibilities, the Trust also supports Tibetan communities and actively engages in educational, humanitarian, and environmental initiatives that embody His Holiness’s vision of universal responsibility,” it said.

headline: Preparing students for life beyond the first job: Bridging the education-employment gap
content: Employees should not be expected to accept humiliation, bullying or unreasonable demands. Organisations must provide realistic workloads, competent managers, proper onboarding and psychologically safe workplaces. Image for representational use. A student may spend 15 to 18 years in education preparing for examinations, qualifications and selection processes. School marks lead to entrance tests, entrance tests to college, and degrees to interviews and, hopefully, a job. When the first offer letter arrives, it is celebrated as the destination. Yet it may only mark the beginning of a different education. What does a young person know about the world they are entering? They may know their subject, but do they understand organisational culture, reporting relationships, teamwork, deadlines, customer expectations and professional communication? Have they experienced constructive criticism, conflicting priorities, a project under pressure or the responsibility of admitting that something is not working? These are everyday realities

headline: Iraqi PM orders federal government to manage oilfields under control of Kurds, Kurds reject move
content: By Kawa Omar, Zainab Elhaj, Maha El Dahan and Maher NazihBAGHDAD, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Iraq’s prime minister has ordered federal authorities to manage oilfields in four provinces under the control of the Kurds, in a risky move likely to further strain relations with their semi-autonomous region after he sought to rein in a heavily armed pro-Iranian militia. The decision announced on Tuesday comes as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi cracks down on Tehran’s most powerful militia proxy in Iraq, Kataib Hezbollah, and senior officials accused of running a years-long smuggling ring that generated hundreds of millions of dollars from oil stolen from the major crude producer. The move reignited long-running disputes between Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) over control of oil, money, territory and trade. The anti-smuggling drive and Zaidi’s push for control over the oilfields put the 41-year-old multimillionaire businessman on a course for direct confrontation with two of the most powerful entrenched groups that have defied Baghdad’s central control for decades: Iran-aligned militias and Kurdish leaders. Both steps also encroach on the vital interests of organisations that have grown hugely powerful throughout the tumultuous decades of ethnosectarian civil war since US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein in 2003, when Zaidi was still a teenager. When one of Zaidi’s predecessors tried to crack down on pro-Iranian militias, a drone attack struck his home in what officials called an assassination attempt.

headline: NGO, alumni object Railways quarters near Vontikoppal School in Mysuru
content: Mysuru: Members of a students' organisation, an NGO and alumni of 108 year old Vontikoppal Government Higher Primary School and Yadavagiri Government High School in Mysuru are up in arms against the construction of staff quarters of South Western Railways (SWR) near the school premises. Members of the schools' alumni association staged a protest on Tuesday along with members of Mysore Grahakara Parishat (MGP) and AIDSO, a students' organisation, urging the authorities to stop the construction. Members of MGP, including founding working president Bhamy Shenoy and working president S K Dinesh claimed, "Railways have not obtained permission from the State government or urban local bodies like Mysore City Corporation (MCC) or Mysore Urban Development Authority (MUDA) for constructing the quarters. They seem to have sought exemption from availing permission under section 11 of the Railways Act, which is only applicable for construction of core essential railway infrastructure such as tracks, bridges, tunnels, stations, yards." .122 Pourakarmikas in Mysuru to get own homes under Gruha Bhagya Yojana.Officials of MCC said that although Section 342 of the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act exempts government constructions on government land the need for permission, South Western Railway should have availed permission. Noting that the Railways did not inform the MCC about the construction, they added, "AC of Zone 4 of MCC has issued notice to SWR officials seeking explanation." "These constructions are also in violation of Parks and Open Spaces Act which applies to all entities, including the Railways, and more so when it is not for essential railway infrastructure. Judicial precedence exists where courts have reinforced this," Shenoy said. "In MUDA Master Plan, this area is earmarked as open space. So Railways must obtain MUDA’s permission for any construction, which is unlikely to be granted. Vontikoppal School is over 100 years old, so its heritage status restricts construction in the immediate surroundings. We have approached Mysuru DC G Lakshmikanth Reddy and Mysuru Division Regional Commissioner Nitesh Patil and others seeking the stoppage of this illegal construction." "The school, built in 1918, currently has 120 students. It has a 100% pass percentage in SSLC. Several noted personalities, including (former CM) S M Krishna have studied in this school. As per The Karnataka Government Educational Institution’s Lands (Protection and Regularisation) Act, 2026 if a school functions in a property for 12 years then it will become its own," he added .Mysuru school launches campaign to build book reading habit.Retired professor Kalachannegowda, members of MGP, including S K Dinesh, Roy Joseph, Ravi Bale, D V Dayanand Sagar, Mansoor Ahmed, Malavika Gubbivani, Rathi Rao and others participated in the protest. Meanwhile, Railway Divisional Commercial Manager and Public Relations Officer Girish Dharmaraj Kalagonda said Railway authorities have already held a meeting with officials of district administration in this regard. "The Railways has dropped the construction of one quarter closer to the school. Railway authorities are building only two staff quarters under the Gathi Shakthi programme to meet the growing demand. These buildings are being constructed in Railway land. This will not affect the school or the ground," he said.

headline: Union Minister of Textiles Shri Giriraj Singh Reviews Textile Sector Initiatives in Tamil Nadu; Emphasises Weaver Welfare, Product Diversification and Export Promotion
content: The Union Minister of Textiles, Shri Giriraj Singh, undertook a series of official engagements in Tamil Nadu on 23 and 24 November 2026, focusing on strengthening the textile and sericulture sectors, promoting industrial development, enhancing weavers’ livelihoods and boosting textile exports. On 24 November 2026, the Minister chaired a review meeting in Chennai with senior officials from the Central and State Governments associated with the handloom sector, Central Silk Board, PM MITRA Park and various verticals of the textile industry. Representatives from industry and allied sectors also participated in the meeting. The meeting was attended by Smt. R. Lilly, IAS, Secretary, Handlooms, Handicrafts, Textiles and Khadi Department, Government of Tamil Nadu; Thiru R. Sadheesh, IAS, Director of Sericulture (Full Additional Charge), Government of Tamil Nadu; Thiru S. A. Raman, IAS, Managing Director, SIPCOT; Tmt. P. Uma Maheswari, IAS, Director of Handlooms, Tamil Nadu; Smt. Swayamprava Pani, Additional Development Commissioner (Handlooms), Ministry of Textiles; Shri Anil Kumar, IRS, Director (Infrastructure), Ministry of Textiles; and Shri P. Sivakumar, IFS, Member Secretary, Central Silk Board, along with other senior officials from the Ministry and associated organisations. The discussions focused on reviewing the progress of the "PM MITRA Park at Virudhunagar, Tamil Nadu"; diversification of silk products in Kanchipuram; enhancement of weavers’ income and revenue; promotion of new-age fibres; and the potential for replicating the successful Kanchipuram cluster model in other textile sectors. The Minister also emphasised the need for a focused and coordinated approach towards promoting textile exports and strengthening India's competitiveness in international markets. Reiterating the Government's commitment to the welfare of the textile sector, Shri Giriraj Singh emphasised the importance of providing better opportunities, improved facilities and necessary support to weavers, artisans and all stakeholders associated with the textile industry across Tamil Nadu, including Chennai. Earlier, on 23 November 2026, following the inauguration of the 27th International Congress on Sericulture and Silk Industry (ISCC-2026) and the Silk Mark Expo 2026 in Chennai, The Minister visited the "Perarignar Anna Handloom Silk Park, Kanchipuram". He inspected the handloom units and viewed the silk products of Prakash Silks & Sarees. He also interacted with weavers and the Board of Directors to review the progress of the project and understand the facilities and opportunities available to the weaving community. Emphasising the importance of strengthening traditional silk weaving, he highlighted the need for improved infrastructure, better facilities and enhanced market opportunities to increase weavers’ income and take Kanchipuram’s rich silk heritage to greater heights.

headline: Indian CVs are shorter than those in US, UK despite detailed education records, study says
content: New Delhi: Almost 98 per cent of Indian jobseekers mention their educational qualifications in their CVs, the highest share alongside the Philippines among the 15 countries studied. However, Indian candidates tend to keep their resumes short, with the average CV running to 1.93 pages.These are among the findings of a study by career company JobLeads, which analysed 1.8 million anonymised CVs uploaded to its free CV review service between July and September 2026. Of these, 2,11,178 CVs were from India, making it the second-largest sample in the study after the US, which was 306,760 CVs.Indian CVs tend to be shorterThe study found that 41 per cent of Indian CVs were one page long, while 39 per cent ran to two pages. Only 21 per cent were three pages or longer.This was lower than the figures for the US and the UK, where 27 per cent and 28 per cent of CVs, respectively, were at least three pages long.South Africa had the longest CVs, with an average length of 2.66 pages. As many as 38 per cent of resumes from the country ran to two pages or more.The global average was two pages. Across all countries, 45 per cent of CVs were one page long, while 22 per cent were three pages or longer. "There is no universal rule on CV length, and what counts as normal varies enormously from one country to the next. India is an interesting case because candidates there include their qualifications more consistently than almost anywhere else measured, and still keep the document to under two pages on average," Jan Hendrik von Ahlen, managing director of JobLeads and a career expert, said in a press release. "No recruiter rejects a CV over its page count, but a third page should earn its place – a publication list or a set of patents, rather than every role a candidate has ever held," he added.Also read: Nearly 197 million Indian workers in jobs vulnerable to AI automation, finds Great Lakes Institute studyIndia among the highest for listing educational qualificationsIndia and the Philippines topped the list for mentioning educational qualifications, with 98 per cent of CVs from both countries including details of candidates' education.The figure stood at 92 per cent in the US and 94 per cent in the UK. Globally, 95 per cent of CVs included an education section.Von Ahlen said there was no fixed rule on a CV's length, as expectations differed from country to country. He also emphasised that recruiters should be able to identify relevant experience, skills and tools quickly."If your CV shows in five seconds why you fit the role, it is doing its job," he said.The study also found significant differences in CV-writing habits across countries. While 82 per cent of French CVs were limited to one page, only 34 per cent of US resumes followed the same format.(Edited by Maryam Hassan)

headline: Kerala To Crack Down On Influencers Promoting Fake Fairness Creams After Reported Kidney Disease
content: Kerala Health Minister K Muraleedharan has called for strict action against social media influencers promoting fake cosmetics and unsafe health products, warning that those involved in misleading advertisements could face legal consequences. The minister has directed the State Drugs Controller to conduct inspections across all districts to curb the sale and online marketing of unapproved cosmetics, fairness creams and protein powders. The move comes after two reported instances of people suffering from kidney disease allegedly following the use of skin-lightening creams. In a statement, Muraleedharan said vloggers who promote harmful products through social media would also be monitored and face legal action, particularly those paid to advertise products that could pose a risk to public health. “Action will also be taken against advertisements that mislead the public by making claims that lack scientific evidence,” the minister said. He further said that licences of establishments selling illegal products would be permanently cancelled and criminal action would be initiated against those responsible. KIDNEY DISEASE CASES TRIGGER ACTION The state-wide crackdown follows claims by a 17-year-old girl and singer Saleem Kodathoor that they developed membranous nephropathy, a kidney disease, after using a skin-lightening cream. Kodathoor claimed that he suffered from the ailment around 10 years ago and had to undergo treatment for several months. The 17-year-old girl recently disclosed her illness, with her doctors reportedly stating that her body had high levels of mercury due to the use of a cream containing dangerous quantities of the chemical. Following these complaints, the health minister directed the State Drugs Controller to inspect establishments across Kerala and take steps to control the sale and online marketing of such products. UNAPPROVED PRODUCTS COMING FROM PAKISTAN, MANGALURU-KASARAGOD REGION Muraleedharan also raised concerns about the source and safety of unapproved cosmetics and health products being sold in the state. “Unapproved cosmetics and health products are being sold in Kerala, by ordering them online from the Mangaluru-Kasaragod region. There are serious concerns about the source, quality and safety of such products,” he said. He added that some products arriving through Pakistan did not even carry basic details such as the manufacturer’s name, date of manufacture and expiry date. “Some products arriving via Pakistan do not even have basic information such as the manufacturer’s name, date of manufacture and expiry date. Action needs to be taken to identify the chain of distribution of such products,” he said. The minister said inspections would specifically cover face sheets, fairness products, creams claiming to enhance skin tone and other beauty products. PROTEIN POWDERS, MUSCLE-BUILDING PRODUCTS ALSO UNDER SCANNER The proposed inspections will not be limited to cosmetics. Products such as pills, ointments and salves marketed through advertisements claiming to increase muscle strength, physical strength and stimulation will also come under scrutiny. Muraleedharan said doctors had warned that certain fake and unsafe products could cause serious health complications affecting the kidneys, liver and nervous system, and could even lead to skin cancer. He pointed out that several products are marketed with promises of enhancing beauty, changing skin tone and delivering quick results, without providing consumers with adequate information about their ingredients and possible health effects. The minister stressed that authorities must examine not just the sale and advertising of such products but also their distribution networks and sources to identify those responsible. MINISTER URGES PUBLIC TO BE CAUTIOUS Muraleedharan appealed to consumers not to be influenced by attractive advertisements and promises of quick results. He urged people to verify whether products have the necessary approvals and carry details about their manufacturers and quality. He also advised that such products should be purchased and used only under the guidance of authorised doctors. The proposed action aims to address the sale and promotion of unapproved products while holding establishments, distributors and social media promoters accountable for misleading consumers and potentially endangering public health.
